chapters.title: Chapter 6: Tax, the Buy Decision and Your Portfolio

lessons.title: Where Real Estate Fits in Your Portfolio

children.text: Two families each have a net worth of ₹3 crore. The Mehtas in Ahmedabad hold ₹2.4 crore in three flats and a plot, plus FDs and gold. The Iyers in Chennai own their ₹1.2 crore home, and the rest is spread across equity mutual funds, debt, REITs and gold. On paper they are equally wealthy. But if either family needs ₹40 lakh next month, loses an income, or sees property prices stall for five years, their experiences will be completely different. The difference is not how much they own. It is how their wealth is arranged. This lesson shows you how to decide where real estate belongs in yours.

body.text: Real estate should be a deliberate slice of your wealth, not the default home for all of it. Treat your own home as a lifestyle decision, then size any investment property by your goals, liquidity needs and what you already own.

children.text: India Is Still Property-Heavy, but Shifting

stats.label: Financial assets in Indian household wealth
stats.context: Among the lowest of 56 markets; UBS Global Wealth Report, 2026

children.text: Indian families still keep most of their wealth in physical assets, but new savings are increasingly flowing into mutual funds and other financial products. For most investors, the practical question is not whether to own property, but how much of their total wealth it should represent, and in what form.
Step 1: Separate Your Home From Your Investments

markDefs.definition: Your net worth excluding the equity in the home you live in: the wealth you could actually deploy, sell or rebalance to meet goals.

The Mehtas' concentration
body.prompt: The Mehtas hold ₹2.4 crore of their ₹3 crore net worth in property. What percentage of their total net worth is in real estate?
body.explanation: ₹2.4 crore ÷ ₹3 crore = 80%. Four of every five rupees they own sit in illiquid, indivisible assets in one city, with limited liquid money for emergencies or opportunities.

body.title: The Iyers' investment real estate
body.prompt: The Iyers have a ₹3 crore net worth, including a ₹1.2 crore home with no loan. Their only other real estate is ₹15 lakh of REITs. What share of their investable net worth is in investment real estate? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Investable net worth: ₹3 crore minus ₹1.2 crore home = ₹1.8 crore. Investment real estate share: ₹15 lakh ÷ ₹1.8 crore = 8.3%. Including their home, total real estate is ₹1.35 crore, or 45% of net worth, which is still substantial but far more balanced than the Mehtas.

children.text: Step 2: Understand What Real Estate Adds, and What It Costs

body.title: Real estate's role in a portfolio

columns.label: What it can contribute
points: Regular income through rent or REIT distributions
A link to inflation through rising rents and construction costs
Returns that do not always move in step with the stock market
A home that provides stability and eventually rent-free living

columns.label: What it costs your portfolio
points: Illiquidity: you cannot raise cash quickly or in parts
Concentration in one city, often your own job market
High transaction costs that make rebalancing expensive
Low net rental yields on direct residential property

children.text: Step 3: Use a Framework, Not a Formula

markDefs.definition: A portfolio approach where most money sits in a diversified, low-cost core, such as equity and debt funds, with smaller satellite positions in specific themes or assets like real estate.

structure: a diversified core of equity and debt aligned with your goals, and real estate as a deliberate satellite. The table below shows illustrative ranges people often consider at different life stages. They are starting points for thinking, not recommendations.

body.text: These ranges exclude the home you live in and are not personal advice. Your right number depends on your income stability, goals, time horizon, existing property, family obligations and tax situation. A family that already lives in its own home and expects to inherit more property may reasonably want very little additional real estate.

children.text: Step 4: Rebalancing When You Cannot Sell a Slice

markDefs.definition: Bringing your asset allocation back towards its target by shifting money from assets that are overweight to those that are underweight.

children.text: is a few clicks. With property, you cannot sell 10% of a flat, and every sale costs lakhs. Families like the Mehtas have two practical levers: sell a whole property, or direct all new savings into other assets until the balance improves.

body.latex: \text{New Savings Needed} = \frac{\text{Real Estate Value}}{\text{Target Share}} - \text{Current Net Worth}
body.caption: This assumes real estate values stay flat and all new savings go into other assets.

body.title: Rebalancing through new savings
body.prompt: The Mehtas want to bring real estate down from 80% to 60% of net worth without selling. Their property is worth ₹2.4 crore and their net worth is ₹3 crore. Assuming property values stay flat, how much new money, in ₹ crore, must they add to non-property assets?
body.explanation: Target net worth: ₹2.4 crore ÷ 60% = ₹4 crore. New savings needed: ₹4 crore minus ₹3 crore = ₹1 crore. Alternatively, selling one flat worth ₹60 lakh would cut property to ₹1.8 crore of ₹3 crore, also 60%, immediately, though with transaction costs and possibly tax.

body.label: The easiest rebalancing tool for property-heavy families
body.value: Stop buying more property and redirect new savings
body.context: Every new rupee sent to equity, debt or REITs gradually reduces concentration, with no stamp duty, brokerage or distress sale. Selling a property can speed things up, but should be planned, not rushed.

body.caption: Choosing a real estate route by goal

Listed REITs; small SM REIT positions
A single strata office or "assured return" unit

Large AIF commitments on top of heavy direct property

body.text: Every route you have studied in this course has a place, but not every route belongs in every portfolio. The same ₹50 lakh can be a sensible diversifier in REITs for one family, and a dangerous extra concentration in a flat for another. Always ask what the investment does to your whole portfolio, not just what it returns on its own.

body.title: The property-heavy family
body.question: A family already holds 75% of its net worth in two flats and a plot. It wants some exposure to commercial real estate income. What is the most sensible way to get it?
options: Buy a strata office unit using a loan against one flat
Buy another plot near an upcoming airport
Allocate a small amount of new savings to listed REITs while directing most new savings to equity and debt funds
Sell all the flats and put everything into one SM REIT scheme
body.explanation: The family's main problem is concentration. A small REIT allocation adds commercial income with liquidity and diversification, while directing most new savings elsewhere steadily reduces property concentration. The other options add leverage, illiquidity or single-asset risk.

body.title: The gentle lever
body.textWithBlank: Property-heavy investors can reduce concentration without selling by directing all new ___ into other asset classes.
body.explanation: Redirecting new savings rebalances gradually without stamp duty, brokerage, capital gains tax or the risk of a rushed sale.

body.title: The Mehtas plan for retirement
body.scenario: Mr and Mrs Mehta, aged 55 and 52, plan to retire in five years. Their ₹3 crore net worth is 80% property: their own home in Satellite, two rented flats and a plot in Sanand. The two flats earn a combined net yield of about 2.5%. They have ₹30 lakh in FDs and ₹30 lakh in gold, and want reliable monthly income in retirement.
body.prompt: How could they restructure their portfolio over the next five years?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Diagnose: 80% in property gives them large wealth but low, lumpy income and little liquidity for a retirement starting in five years.
2. Keep the home: their Satellite home provides stability in retirement and should stay.
3. Review the plot: a non-income-producing plot contributes nothing to retirement income. Selling it in a good market, after checking capital gains tax and exemptions, could free up significant capital.
4. Review the rented flats: at about 2.5% net yield, they produce modest income. Selling one, patiently, and reinvesting could raise income and liquidity.
5. Redirect proceeds: into a mix suited to retirement, such as debt instruments and senior citizen schemes for stable income, listed REITs for property-linked income, and a diversified equity allocation to protect against inflation over a long retirement.
6. Stop adding property: all new savings over the next five years should go to financial assets.
7. Plan tax and timing: phase any sales, compare the 12.5% and indexed options, and consider exemptions, with help from a tax professional and a SEBI-registered investment adviser.

body.title: Review Where Real Estate Sits in Your Portfolio
steps: List every property, REIT, real estate fund and AIF you own, at current value
Calculate total real estate as a share of net worth
Calculate investment real estate as a share of investable net worth, excluding your home
Check how much of your wealth could be turned into cash within a month
Note whether your property and your income depend on the same city or industry
Decide a target range for investment real estate based on your goals and life stage
If you are above it, redirect new savings and plan any sales patiently
Review the allocation once a year

points: Indian households remain property-heavy, with financial assets at just 25.8% of wealth, but SIP flows show savings shifting.
Separate your own home from investment real estate, and measure both total and investable concentration.
Real estate can add income, inflation linkage and diversification, but brings illiquidity, concentration and high transaction costs.
Use a core-satellite approach: a diversified core of equity and debt, with real estate as a deliberate, sized satellite.
Property-heavy families can rebalance by redirecting new savings, or by planned sales of non-core property.
Match the route to the goal: a home for stability, REITs for income, and small, careful positions in funds, SM REITs or AIFs.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not personalised investment advice. Allocation ranges and family examples are illustrative, and the right mix depends on your circumstances. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before changing your portfolio.
